item.title: CAPTCHA Providers Compared for Login Pages: reCAPTCHA, hCaptcha, Turnstile, GeeTest and Alibaba Cloud in Casdoor
item.description: Compare reCAPTCHA, hCaptcha, Cloudflare Turnstile, GeeTest, Alibaba Cloud Captcha and the built-in captcha for login and sign-up pages, and use them in Casdoor.
item.content:encoded:
For most sign-in and sign-up pages on the global internet, Cloudflare Turnstile is the easiest pick: the free plan has no cap on challenges, and its default mode shows a checkbox only to risky visitors. If many of your users are in mainland China, use Alibaba Cloud Captcha or GeeTest instead, because Cloudflare says Turnstile is not supported there. If you need the captcha to work without any outside service, use the built-in image captcha of Casdoor. Casdoor supports all of these, plus Google reCAPTCHA (v2 and v3) and hCaptcha, as captcha providers, and you pick when the captcha appears per application.

The comparison​

Pricing and availability below were checked against each vendor's own site on 2026-11-02. Where a vendor does not publish a number, the table says so instead of guessing.

ProviderWhat the user seesInvisible modeData and privacyFree tier and pricingMainland ChinaCasdoor type
Casdoor defaultTypes five digits from an imageNoGenerated and checked by your Casdoor server; no third partyFree, part of CasdoorWorks, no outside callDefault
Google reCAPTCHA v2Checkbox; some users get an image challengev2 also has an invisible variant that challenges only suspicious trafficGoogle; sets the _GRECAPTCHA cookie for risk analysisEssentials tier free up to 10,000 assessments per month per organization; Premium is $8 flat up to 100,000, then $1 per 1,000Google says to use www.recaptcha.net where www.google.com is not accessiblereCAPTCHA, reCAPTCHA v2 (checkbox)
Google reCAPTCHA v3Nothing; returns a scoreYesSame as v2Same as v2Same as v2reCAPTCHA v3
hCaptchaCheckbox with image challenges on the free planPassive mode on Pro ("99.9% passive") and a no-CAPTCHA mode on EnterpriseSays the free plan complies with GDPR, CCPA, LGPD and PIPL; certifies to the EU-U.S. Data Privacy FrameworkBasic is free; Pro is $139 per month (or $99 per month billed yearly) with 100,000 evaluations, then $0.99 per 1,000; Enterprise through salesNot documented by hCaptchahCaptcha
Cloudflare TurnstileManaged mode shows a checkbox only when neededNon-interactive and Invisible widget modesCloudflare says it processes only the data strictly necessary and does not read form entries; no Cloudflare proxy requiredFree plan: unlimited challenges, up to 20 widgets; Enterprise through salesCloudflare: "not supported in Mainland China"Cloudflare Turnstile
GeeTest CAPTCHA v4One-click, slide puzzle, text click, match-threeNot listed on the v4 product pageChinese vendor; product-specific privacy policyNo public price list; 30-day free trial, then salesChinese vendorGEETEST
Alibaba Cloud Captcha 2.0One-click, slider, jigsaw, image restorationTraceless mode in the Standard and Enterprise editionsRuns on Alibaba CloudPay as you go: 0.005 CNY per call in mainland China, 0.007 CNY outside; subscription editions and resource packages also availableYes; Casdoor verifies against the Shanghai region endpointAliyun Captcha

Two notes on the reCAPTCHA rows. Google has moved reCAPTCHA into Google Cloud Fraud Defense with Essentials, Premium and Enterprise tiers, and the free allowance of 10,000 assessments is pooled across the whole Google Cloud organization. Casdoor talks to reCAPTCHA with a site key and secret key through the standard siteverify endpoint, and it loads the script from recaptcha.net rather than google.com, for both the browser script and server-side verification.

Which one to pick​

Global SaaS​

Start with Cloudflare Turnstile. The free plan does not meter challenges, the Managed mode keeps most users from clicking anything, and you do not need to route your site through Cloudflare. If you already run on Google Cloud and want reCAPTCHA's risk signals, reCAPTCHA is fine, but watch the 10,000 free assessments: a busy sign-in page or an SMS-pumping attack can pass that in a day. hCaptcha is the other common choice; its free plan always shows a challenge, and the passive modes are paid.

An app with users in mainland China​

Turnstile is out, by Cloudflare's own documentation. For reCAPTCHA, Google documents www.recaptcha.net as the domain to use when www.google.com is not reachable, and Casdoor already uses it, but you should still test from your users' networks before you depend on it. hCaptcha publishes no statement about China, so the same advice applies.

The two safe picks are Alibaba Cloud Captcha and GeeTest. Alibaba Cloud publishes per-call prices and lets you start pay-as-you-go; its traceless mode (in Casdoor, use the Popup sub type for it) gets close to the invisible experience of Turnstile. GeeTest sells through its sales team after a 30-day trial. If you serve both China and the rest of the world from one Casdoor, remember that an application has one captcha provider, so split the audiences into two applications if they need different captchas.

Privacy-sensitive users in the EU​

Every hosted captcha sends some data about the visitor's browser to the vendor. If your legal team wants no third party in the sign-in path at all, the Casdoor default captcha is the only option in the table that keeps everything on your own server. Among the hosted ones, Turnstile and hCaptcha both describe privacy as part of the product (data limited to what the check needs, GDPR and the EU-U.S. Data Privacy Framework respectively). reCAPTCHA sets a _GRECAPTCHA cookie; Google notes that serving from www.recaptcha.net avoids other cookies that www.google.com may set. Whichever you pick, list it in your privacy notice.

Self-hosted, intranet or offline​

Use the default captcha. It needs no keys and no outbound network access, so it works in air-gapped installs. Pair it with the Internet-Only rule (below) so that people on the office network never see it, while requests from the public internet still do.

The default captcha is the weakest of the group against automated solvers, since it is a plain distorted-digits image. For a public, high-traffic sign-in page, combine it with multi-factor authentication or move users to passwordless sign-in, which removes the password guessing that captchas exist to slow down.

How CAPTCHA works in Casdoor​

You add a provider with Category set to Captcha and one of these types: Default, reCAPTCHA, reCAPTCHA v2, reCAPTCHA v3, hCaptcha, Cloudflare Turnstile, GEETEST or Aliyun Captcha. Then you add it to an application on the Providers tab. An application can hold only one captcha provider; Casdoor refuses to save a second one. Setup steps for each vendor are in the captcha provider docs.

Where Casdoor asks for it​

The same provider guards several actions, and Casdoor checks the token on the server, not only in the browser:

  • Password sign-in.
  • Sign-up form submission.
  • Sending a verification code by email or SMS, which covers the code step of sign-up, the forgot-password page and code-based sign-in. This is the protection against bots that burn your SMS budget.

When Casdoor asks for it​

The Rule of the captcha provider in the application decides when it appears:

RuleBehavior
NoneNever; the captcha is off
DynamicOnly after the user's failed sign-ins reach the application's Failed signin limit
AlwaysEvery time
Internet-OnlyFor requests from public IP addresses; not for private, loopback or other non-public addresses

Dynamic is the gentlest setting for sign-in: honest users never see a challenge, and someone guessing passwords hits one after a few failures. It only applies to accounts that already exist, though. A sign-up, or a code sent to an address that has no account yet, does not trigger it. If SMS or email abuse at sign-up is your concern, use Always or Internet-Only.

Where it appears on the page​

On the application's sign-in items, the Captcha item has its own rule: Pop up shows the captcha in a dialog when it is needed, and Inline puts it directly on the page. See Change the captcha. Alibaba Cloud Captcha has an extra Sub type: Embed shows it inside the Casdoor dialog, and Popup hands control to Alibaba Cloud's own popup, which is what traceless scenes need.

Use the Preview button on the provider page to check the keys before you turn the rule on.

References​

  • Google reCAPTCHA versions: https://developers.google.com/recaptcha/docs/versions
  • Google reCAPTCHA FAQ (recaptcha.net, _GRECAPTCHA cookie): https://developers.google.com/recaptcha/docs/faq
  • reCAPTCHA billing in Google Cloud Fraud Defense (checked 2026-11-02): https://docs.cloud.google.com/recaptcha/docs/billing-information
  • hCaptcha pricing (checked 2026-11-02): https://www.hcaptcha.com/pricing
  • hCaptcha privacy policy: https://www.hcaptcha.com/privacy
  • Cloudflare Turnstile overview: https://developers.cloudflare.com/turnstile/
  • Cloudflare Turnstile plans (checked 2026-11-02): https://developers.cloudflare.com/turnstile/plans/
  • Cloudflare China Network FAQ (Turnstile in mainland China): https://developers.cloudflare.com/china-network/faq/
  • GeeTest CAPTCHA v4 (checked 2026-11-02): https://www.geetest.com/adaptive-captcha
  • Alibaba Cloud Captcha 2.0 overview: https://help.aliyun.com/zh/captcha/captcha2-0/product-overview/what-is-alibaba-cloud-captcha-2

item.title: MailHog vs Mailpit: Testing Verification and Password Reset Emails with Casdoor
item.description: MailHog vs Mailpit: both listen on SMTP port 1025 and web UI port 8025. Compare maintenance, Docker images and test APIs, then point Casdoor at either one.
item.content:encoded:
MailHog and Mailpit are both fake SMTP servers for development: they accept every message, keep it, and show it in a web UI instead of delivering it. Both use the same default ports, SMTP on 1025 and the web UI and API on 8025, so the SMTP address is smtp://127.0.0.1:1025 and the inbox is at http://127.0.0.1:8025 for either one. The difference is maintenance: MailHog's last release, v1.0.1, came out in August 2020, while Mailpit released v1.33.0 on October 31, 2026. For a new project, use Mailpit. Casdoor sends to both through a plain SMTP provider, so you can test sign-up codes, password reset emails and magic links without a real mail account.

MailHog vs Mailpit at a glance​

MailHogMailpit
Latest releasev1.0.1, 2020-08-11v1.33.0, 2026-10-31
Last commit on the default branch2022-08-022026-10-31
LicenseMITMIT
Default SMTP port10251025
Default web UI and API port80258025
Docker imagemailhog/mailhog, amd64 onlyaxllent/mailpit, amd64, arm64 and 386
HTTP APIv1 and v2: list, get, delete, search by from, to or containingv1: list, get, delete, search with filters such as to: and subject:, latest message shortcut
Default storageIn memoryTemporary SQLite database, deleted on exit
Persistent storageMongoDB or MaildirSQLite file (MP_DATABASE) or rqlite
Message limitNone documentedKeeps the newest 500 by default (MP_MAX_MESSAGES)
HTML check, link check, spam checkNoYes
Webhook on new mailNoYes (MP_WEBHOOK_URL)
SMTP TLSNot offeredOptional STARTTLS or SSL/TLS
Failure injectionJimChaos
Release a message to a real SMTP serverYesYes
POP3 serverNoYes, optional
Basic auth for the web UIYesYes

Docker Hub counts show that many people still pull MailHog. That reflects old tutorials and CI files, not activity: an open issue on the MailHog repository titled "THIS PROJECT IS DEAD!" has a 2023 reply from the author saying he no longer has time to maintain it. Mailpit's README describes itself as inspired by MailHog and points to that same comment.

The image architecture matters more than it looks. On an Apple Silicon laptop or an ARM CI runner, mailhog/mailhog runs only under emulation, while axllent/mailpit has a native arm64 image.

Run either one with Docker​

MailHog:

docker run -d --name mailhog -p 1025:1025 -p 8025:8025 mailhog/mailhog

Mailpit:

docker run -d --name mailpit -p 1025:1025 -p 8025:8025 axllent/mailpit

Mailpit keeps mail in a temporary database that disappears when the container stops. To keep it across restarts, mount a volume and set MP_DATABASE:

docker run -d --name mailpit \
  -v "$PWD/mailpit-data:/data" \
  -e MP_DATABASE=/data/mailpit.db \
  -p 1025:1025 -p 8025:8025 \
  axllent/mailpit

Without Docker, brew install mailhog and brew install mailpit both work on macOS, and Mailpit ships static binaries for Windows, Linux and macOS on its releases page.

In GitHub Actions, run it as a service container next to your test job:

services:
  mailpit:
    image: axllent/mailpit
    ports:
      - 1025:1025
      - 8025:8025

Point Casdoor at MailHog or Mailpit​

Casdoor has no separate provider type for MailHog or Mailpit, and it doesn't need one. The Default email type sends over SMTP, and both tools are SMTP servers.

  1. As a global administrator, add a provider in the admin or built-in organization.
  2. Définissez Category sur Email et Type sur Default.
  3. Set Host to where the tool runs and Port to 1025.
  4. Leave Username and Password empty.
  5. Click Test SMTP Connection, then Send Testing Email, and check the web UI on port 8025.

The step-by-step pages with screenshots are Test email with MailHog and Test email with Mailpit.

A few details decide whether this works on the first try:

Leave SSL mode on Auto, or set it to Disable. In Auto, Casdoor uses implicit TLS only on port 465 and upgrades with STARTTLS only if the server offers it. Neither MailHog nor a default Mailpit offers STARTTLS on port 1025, so the connection stays plain. Don't choose Enable: that forces implicit TLS, and the handshake fails against a plain-text server. The SSL mode table has the full behavior.

Leave the credentials empty. Casdoor logs in to the SMTP server only when Username is set. If you fill it in, Go's PLAIN authentication refuses to send the password over an unencrypted connection unless the host is localhost, so a MailHog at 192.168.x.x fails with an authentication error even though MailHog would accept any login. Mailpit by default doesn't ask for authentication at all.

Use the right host. 127.0.0.1 works only when Casdoor and the mail catcher run on the same machine. If both run in Docker Compose, use the service name, such as mailpit, as the host.

Use a global provider. A provider owned by an ordinary organization may only reach Internet addresses, so it can't connect to 127.0.0.1 or a private IP. Providers in admin or built-in aren't restricted. See Which addresses a provider can reach.

Set origin for links. Verification codes work right away. Password reset links and magic links need Casdoor to know its public URL, through origin in conf/app.conf or a request on a loopback host. Otherwise the reset link is dropped from the email and magic links fail. See Templates.

Finally, add the provider to your application in Add providers to an application so sign-up and password reset actually use it.

Read the verification code in an automated test​

Casdoor's verification codes are six digits, and the default template reads "Here is your code: " followed by the code. An end-to-end test signs up a user, asks Casdoor to send the code, then reads it from the mail catcher's API.

With Mailpit, search by recipient and open the newest match. GET /api/v1/search returns matches newest first, and GET /api/v1/message/{ID} returns the parsed Text and HTML bodies:

import { request } from "@playwright/test";

const MAILPIT = process.env.MAILPIT_URL ?? "http://127.0.0.1:8025";

export async function latestCode(to: string): Promise<string> {
  const api = await request.newContext({ baseURL: MAILPIT });
  for (let i = 0; i < 20; i++) {
    const res = await api.get("/api/v1/search", {
      params: { query: `to:"${to}"`, limit: "1" },
    });
    const { messages } = await res.json();
    if (messages.length > 0) {
      const msg = await (await api.get(`/api/v1/message/${messages[0].ID}`)).json();
      const match = (msg.Text || msg.HTML).match(/code: (\d{6})/);
      if (match) return match[1];
    }
    await new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 500));
  }
  throw new Error(`no verification email for ${to}`);
}

If only one test sends mail at a time, GET /api/v1/message/latest skips the search step. Before each test, DELETE /api/v1/messages with no body clears the inbox.

With MailHog, the closest call is GET /api/v2/search?kind=to&query=<address>. Messages come back newest first in items, and the body is in items[0].Content.Body:

const res = await api.get("/api/v2/search", {
  params: { kind: "to", query: to, limit: "1" },
});
const { items } = await res.json();
const body: string = items[0]?.Content.Body ?? "";

Content.Body is the raw MIME body. Casdoor sends quoted-printable, so = becomes =3D and long lines get soft breaks ending in =. Decode it first, or keep the code near the start of a short template. Clear MailHog with DELETE /api/v1/messages.

Migrating from MailHog to Mailpit​

Because the ports match, most migrations are a one-line change in docker-compose.yml: replace mailhog/mailhog with axllent/mailpit. Casdoor's provider keeps the same host and port. What does change:

  • Settings. MailHog reads MH_* variables; Mailpit reads MP_*. If you used MH_STORAGE=maildir or MongoDB, move to MP_DATABASE.
  • Test helpers. Mailpit has no /api/v2 endpoints. Rewrite calls to /api/v2/messages and /api/v2/search for /api/v1/messages and /api/v1/search, and read messages[].ID plus Text or HTML instead of items[].Content.Body. The quoted-printable decoding goes away.
  • Search syntax. kind=to&query=a@example.com becomes query=to:"a@example.com".
  • Failure injection. Jim has no flags in Mailpit; use Chaos.
  • Authentication. If an app insists on logging in over plain SMTP, start Mailpit with MP_SMTP_AUTH_ACCEPT_ANY=1 and MP_SMTP_AUTH_ALLOW_INSECURE=1. For Casdoor, leaving the credentials empty is simpler.
  • Retention. Mailpit prunes to the newest 500 messages by default. Raise MP_MAX_MESSAGES if a long test run needs more.

Going to production​

MailHog and Mailpit never deliver mail to real inboxes unless you release messages by hand, so production needs a real provider. In Casdoor you swap the provider, not the templates. The email templates, the %s code placeholder and the <reset-link> block stay the same:

  • Any SMTP server with the Default type, described in Email providers
  • SendGrid and Resend through their APIs
  • Brevo through its SMTP relay
  • Azure Communication Services
  • Your own HTTP endpoint with Custom HTTP Email

A common setup keeps Mailpit in development and CI and the real provider in production. Each environment points its application at a different provider, so the sign-up flow you test is the one that ships.

References​

  • MailHog repository and README: https://github.com/mailhog/MailHog
  • MailHog configuration and API v1/v2 docs: https://github.com/mailhog/MailHog/tree/master/docs
  • MailHog maintenance comment: https://github.com/mailhog/MailHog/issues/442#issuecomment-1493415258
  • Mailpit repository and README: https://github.com/axllent/mailpit
  • Mailpit documentation (Docker, storage, SMTP, webhook, search filters): https://mailpit.axllent.org/docs/
  • Mailpit API v1 reference: https://mailpit.axllent.org/docs/api-v1/
  • Casdoor email provider code: https://github.com/casdoor/casdoor/tree/master/email

item.title: MCP OAuth Redirect URIs for Cursor, Claude and ChatGPT: Registering MCP Clients in Casdoor
item.description: The OAuth callback URLs that Cursor, Claude and ChatGPT use for MCP servers, where claude_desktop_config.json lives, and how to register each client in Casdoor.
item.content:encoded:
Every MCP client sends its own redirect URI when it signs in to an OAuth-protected MCP server. Cursor desktop uses http://localhost:8787/callback (releases before mid-2026 used cursor://anysphere.cursor-mcp/oauth/callback), Cursor on the web and Cursor Cloud Agents use https://www.cursor.com/agents/mcp/oauth/callback, claude.ai, Claude Desktop connectors, Claude mobile and Cowork use https://claude.ai/api/mcp/auth_callback, and ChatGPT uses https://chatgpt.com/connector_platform_oauth_redirect or a per-connection https://chatgpt.com/connector/oauth/<callback-id>. If you turn on dynamic client registration in Casdoor, you don't enter any of these: the clients register themselves or hand Casdoor a client ID metadata document. You add them to Redirect URLs only when you create a Casdoor application for a client by hand.

Redirect URIs by client​

ClientRedirect URIHow it gets a client ID from CasdoorNotes
Cursor desktop (current)http://localhost:8787/callbackDCR, or auth.CLIENT_ID in mcp.jsonFixed port 8787
Cursor web and Cloud Agentshttps://www.cursor.com/agents/mcp/oauth/callbackDCR, or auth.CLIENT_IDWith DCR, the desktop app registers this URI and the localhost one
Cursor desktop (older releases)cursor://anysphere.cursor-mcp/oauth/callbackDCR, or auth.CLIENT_IDCursor made the loopback URI the default in July 2026
claude.ai, Claude Desktop connectors, Claude mobile, Coworkhttps://claude.ai/api/mcp/auth_callbackCIMD, then DCR, or a client ID entered in the custom connector dialogAnthropic's servers make the requests
Claude Codehttp://localhost:<port>/callback and http://127.0.0.1:<port>/callbackCIMDThe port changes per session
Claude Desktop through mcp-remotehttp://localhost:<port>/oauth/callbackDCRThe port is derived from the server URL
ChatGPThttps://chatgpt.com/connector_platform_oauth_redirect, or https://chatgpt.com/connector/oauth/<callback-id>CIMD, DCR, or a predefined clientCopy the exact value from ChatGPT

These values come from the vendors' documentation as of November 2, 2026 (see References). Clients change them. When a sign-in fails, read the redirect_uri parameter of the authorization request in the browser's address bar and compare it with what Casdoor has.

The table applies in two setups: the MCP server built into Casdoor at /api/mcp, and your own MCP server that uses Casdoor as its authorization server. In both, the client finds Casdoor through protected resource metadata (RFC 9728) and gets its client ID from Casdoor.

Option 1: let clients register themselves​

Casdoor supports dynamic client registration (RFC 7591) at /api/oauth/register, and client ID metadata documents (CIMD), where the client_id is an HTTPS URL of a JSON document that lists the client's redirect URIs. One switch controls both: Enable dynamic client registration on the organization. It is off by default, for every organization including built-in.

With the switch on for built-in, the discovery document shows what the clients look for:

curl -s https://your-casdoor.com/.well-known/openid-configuration | jq '{
  registration_endpoint,
  client_id_metadata_document_supported,
  code_challenge_methods_supported,
  token_endpoint_auth_methods_supported,
  authorization_response_iss_parameter_supported
}'
{
  "registration_endpoint": "https://your-casdoor.com/api/oauth/register",
  "client_id_metadata_document_supported": true,
  "code_challenge_methods_supported": ["S256"],
  "token_endpoint_auth_methods_supported": ["client_secret_basic", "client_secret_post", "private_key_jwt", "none"],
  "authorization_response_iss_parameter_supported": true
}

Each client then picks its method:

  • Claude uses CIMD only when the metadata has both client_id_metadata_document_supported: true and none in token_endpoint_auth_methods_supported. Casdoor has both once the switch is on, so Claude identifies itself with a document URL and Casdoor creates an application named cimd_.... Otherwise Claude falls back to DCR.
  • ChatGPT prefers CIMD, with the client_id https://chatgpt.com/oauth/client.json (or a per-callback variant), and uses DCR when CIMD isn't available.
  • Cursor registers through DCR as a public client without a secret. Cursor's documentation doesn't mention CIMD.
  • mcp-remote registers through DCR.

The redirect URIs come from the registration request or the metadata document, so there is nothing to type. Registered clients run under a restricted role and their tokens can't call the management API. See Dynamic client registration for the full rules and the organization a client lands in.

Option 2: create an application for the client​

If you keep registration off, create one application per client, so that you can revoke them separately:

  1. Dans la console d'administration Casdoor, allez dans Identity > Applications et ajoutez une application, par exemple cursor-mcp.
  2. Add the client's redirect URIs from the table to Redirect URLs. For Cursor, add all three, because different Cursor installs send different ones.
  3. Set Category to Agent. See Set up Casdoor for your MCP server for scopes and grant types.
  4. Give the Client ID to the client.

A client secret is optional for these clients. Casdoor accepts an authorization code exchange without a secret when the request used PKCE, and Cursor, Claude and ChatGPT all use PKCE with S256. If a client does send a secret, it must be the right one.

Where the client ID goes:

  • Cursor: an auth object in ~/.cursor/mcp.json or .cursor/mcp.json. With a static CLIENT_ID, the Cursor desktop app sends only its localhost redirect URI.

    {
      "mcpServers": {
        "casdoor": {
          "url": "https://your-casdoor.com/api/mcp",
          "auth": {
            "CLIENT_ID": "${env:CASDOOR_MCP_CLIENT_ID}",
            "scopes": ["application:read", "user:read"]
          }
        }
      }
    }

  • Claude: the OAuth client ID field in the custom connector dialog. Register https://claude.ai/api/mcp/auth_callback.

  • ChatGPT: ChatGPT also works with predefined OAuth clients. Copy the redirect URI from the MCP server's management page in ChatGPT, since which of the two forms it uses depends on the authorization server.

Step-by-step guides: Cursor, Claude Desktop, ChatGPT.

How Casdoor matches redirect URIs​

Casdoor compares the redirect_uri of a request with each entry in Redirect URLs:

  • The scheme, the host and the path must match. The query string isn't compared.
  • The port must match, except on loopback hosts. When both URIs use the same loopback host (localhost, 127.0.0.1 or ::1), Casdoor ignores the port, as RFC 8252 asks for native apps. localhost and 127.0.0.1 are different hosts, so Claude Code needs both http://localhost/callback and http://127.0.0.1/callback.
  • A redirect URI on a subdomain of a registered host also matches, so https://example.com/cb accepts https://app.example.com/cb. Register the most specific host you can.
  • Custom schemes such as cursor:// match by the same rules. javascript:, data: and vbscript: URIs are always rejected.

Because the loopback port is ignored, an mcp-remote or Claude Code registration keeps working when the local port changes between sessions.

Where claude_desktop_config.json lives​

The MCP documentation gives these paths. In Claude Desktop, Settings > Developer > Edit Config opens the file and creates it if it's missing.

Operating systemPath
macOS~/Library/Application Support/Claude/claude_desktop_config.json
Windows%APPDATA%\Claude\claude_desktop_config.json
Linux~/.config/Claude/claude_desktop_config.json

Claude Desktop reaches a remote MCP server in one of two ways, and they use different redirect URIs:

  • As a connector, added in Claude's connector settings. Anthropic's servers run the OAuth flow, the redirect URI is https://claude.ai/api/mcp/auth_callback, and Casdoor must be reachable from the internet.

  • Through claude_desktop_config.json, with mcp-remote as a local bridge. The OAuth flow runs on your computer, and the redirect URI is http://localhost:<port>/oauth/callback:

    {
      "mcpServers": {
        "casdoor": {
          "command": "npx",
          "args": ["mcp-remote", "https://your-casdoor.com/api/mcp"]
        }
      }
    }

Quit Claude Desktop completely and start it again after you edit the file.

Hosted clients need a public Casdoor​

ChatGPT and Claude connectors call your MCP server and Casdoor from their vendors' servers, not from your computer. Casdoor must be reachable over public HTTPS with a valid certificate. Anthropic's requests come from 160.79.104.0/21, if you filter by IP. Cursor desktop, Claude Code and mcp-remote run the flow locally, so a Casdoor on your network works for them.

Two more things hosted clients check, which Casdoor already does:

  • Issuer in the response (RFC 9207): ChatGPT rejects an authorization response without the right iss, and uses its stable redirect URI only with authorization servers that meet its RFC 9207 requirements. Casdoor advertises the support in its metadata and adds iss to the redirect.
  • Resource indicators (RFC 8707): ChatGPT sends resource with the MCP server URL on the authorization and token requests. Casdoor puts that value in the aud claim of the access token, and your MCP server should check it. See MCP authentication for the discovery flow.

Related reading on www.casdoor.com: OAuth for AI agents and authorization servers for MCP.

References​

  • Cursor: Model Context Protocol (MCP), section "Static OAuth for remote servers"
  • Cursor forum: OAuth redirect URI changed from cursor:// to http://localhost

item.title: Nginx CAS Authentication and SSO: Protecting Any App Behind Nginx with Casdoor
item.description: Add CAS, OIDC or auth_request login in front of any app behind nginx with Casdoor: forward auth, OAuth2 Proxy, an nginx module, CAS clients and MFA compared.
item.content:encoded:
Open-source nginx has no CAS module, so "nginx CAS authentication" in practice means one of two setups. Either nginx asks an authentication service about every request through its auth_request module, and Casdoor answers (directly at /api/forward-auth, or through casdoor-forward-auth or OAuth2 Proxy), or the app behind nginx is itself a CAS client and talks to Casdoor's CAS server endpoints. If you can rebuild nginx, the Casdoor nginx module runs the login inside nginx, and if you'd rather not run nginx at all, Casdoor's site proxy can sit in front of the app. In every case the login page is Casdoor's, so one SSO session, one set of permissions and one MFA policy cover all the apps.

The options at a glance​

OptionLogin logic runs inWhat nginx needsProtocol to CasdoorWho gets inPick it when
Casdoor forward authCasdoor, /api/forward-authauth_requestCasdoor session cookie on the app's domainApplication permissions, checked again at least once a minutenginx is already in front and you want no extra service
casdoor-forward-authA small Go serviceauth_requestOIDC authorization codeCasdoor roles or groups, per locationOne session cookie shared by many subdomains
OAuth2 ProxyOAuth2 Proxyauth_requestOIDCallowed_groups, email domainsYou already run OAuth2 Proxy
casdoor-nginx-modulenginx itselfA compiled moduleOIDC with PKCE, tokens verified locallyAny signed-in user of the appNo extra process, plus bearer tokens for APIs
CAS client in the appThe appNothing, it only proxiesCAS 1.0, 2.0, 3.0Whatever the app does with the attributesThe app already supports CAS
Casdoor site proxyCasdoor on ports 80 and 443No nginxCasdoor sessionApplication permissionsNothing else is in front of the app

The first three differ only in who answers nginx's subrequest.

Why there is no "nginx CAS module"​

CAS is a conversation between an application and the CAS server: the app sends the browser to the server's /login with a service URL, gets a service ticket back on that URL, and validates the ticket with a server-to-server call. Apache httpd has Apereo's mod_auth_cas for doing this at the web server, but nginx has no CAS module among its official modules. For nginx, the standard building block is ngx_http_auth_request_module: before serving a request, nginx sends a subrequest to a URL you choose. A 2xx answer lets the request through, 401 or 403 denies it with that code, and any other code is an error.

To the user, a CAS login and an OIDC login look the same: a redirect to the Casdoor login page and back. So for an app without CAS support, the practical answer is OIDC at the nginx layer. Background on the protocol: What is CAS.

The auth_request module is not built by default: add --with-http_auth_request_module when compiling, or check nginx -V on a packaged nginx.

Option 1: Casdoor's own forward auth​

Casdoor can answer nginx's subrequest itself. You add a Site in Casdoor whose Domain is the app's domain and whose Casdoor app is the application users sign in to, and add https://app.example.com/caswaf-handler to that application's Redirect URLs. Host and port can stay empty, since the traffic doesn't pass through Casdoor.

Because auth_request can't follow a redirect, Casdoor answers an unauthenticated subrequest with 401 and puts the login URL in Location. nginx turns that into a 302:

server {
    server_name app.example.com;

    proxy_buffer_size 16k;
    proxy_buffers 8 16k;

    location = /caswaf-handler {
        proxy_pass http://casdoor:8000/api/forward-auth;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Host $http_host;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Uri $request_uri;
    }

    location = /casdoor-auth {
        internal;
        proxy_pass http://casdoor:8000/api/forward-auth;
        proxy_pass_request_body off;
        proxy_set_header Content-Length "";
        proxy_set_header X-Original-URL $scheme://$http_host$request_uri;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Method $request_method;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
    }

    location / {
        auth_request /casdoor-auth;
        auth_request_set $casdoor_redirect $upstream_http_location;
        auth_request_set $casdoor_user $upstream_http_x_forwarded_user;
        auth_request_set $casdoor_email $upstream_http_x_forwarded_email;
        auth_request_set $casdoor_groups $upstream_http_x_forwarded_groups;
        error_page 401 =302 $casdoor_redirect;

        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-User $casdoor_user;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Email $casdoor_email;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Groups $casdoor_groups;
        proxy_pass http://app:3000;
    }
}

The backend receives the user in X-Forwarded-User, X-Forwarded-Email and X-Forwarded-Groups. Access follows a permission on the application, checked again at least once a minute, so a disabled user loses access quickly. The site's Public paths (webhooks, health checks) pass without a login.

See Using your own reverse proxy for the reference and Add login to an app without OIDC for a Grafana walkthrough. The app must only be reachable through nginx, or anyone can send X-Forwarded-User themselves.

Option 2: casdoor-forward-auth or OAuth2 Proxy​

If you would rather not create a Casdoor site for each app, run a small service that does the OIDC flow against Casdoor and answers the subrequest.

casdoor-forward-auth is Casdoor's standalone service for this (it replaced traefik-casdoor-auth). It keeps the user in a signed cookie with no server state. For nginx it exposes /verify, which answers 200 with identity headers or 401, and nginx redirects to its /login on 401:

server {
    server_name app.example.com;

    location = /_casdoor_verify {
        internal;
        proxy_pass http://casdoor-forward-auth:9999/verify?groups=built-in/dev;
        proxy_pass_request_body off;
        proxy_set_header Content-Length "";
    }

    location @casdoor_login {
        return 302 https://auth.example.com/login?rd=$scheme://$http_host$request_uri;
    }

    location / {
        auth_request /_casdoor_verify;
        error_page 401 = @casdoor_login;

        auth_request_set $casdoor_user $upstream_http_x_forwarded_user;
        auth_request_set $casdoor_roles $upstream_http_x_forwarded_roles;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-User $casdoor_user;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Roles $casdoor_roles;
        proxy_pass http://app:8080;
    }
}

The roles and groups query parameters on the verify URL restrict each app to holders of a Casdoor role or members of a group; signed-in users without them get 403. Roles and groups are read at login and kept for the session, so changes apply after the user signs in again. Setting COOKIE_DOMAIN=example.com lets one login cover every subdomain. The Traefik guide covers the same service for Traefik.

OAuth2 Proxy works the same way with provider = "oidc" and oidc_issuer_url set to your Casdoor URL. Its /oauth2/auth endpoint returns 202 or 401, user and email headers need --set-xauthrequest, and the forwarded-header handling in its nginx example requires --reverse-proxy. Two Casdoor settings matter: use the JWT-Standard token format, or users with an unverified email are rejected, and keep the profile scope so groups and roles are returned. See OAuth2 Proxy with Casdoor and the nginx community edition guide.

Option 3: the Casdoor nginx module​

casdoor-nginx-module does the login inside nginx, without a separate process. Browsers without a session go to Casdoor's login page; the module exchanges the code with PKCE, verifies the access token's signature, exp, aud and type against the Casdoor certificate, and keeps the user in a signed cookie. API clients can send Authorization: Bearer with a Casdoor access token, verified locally without a call to Casdoor.

It needs nginx 1.22 or newer and OpenSSL 1.1.1 or newer. You can build it as a dynamic module against the nginx you already run:

./configure --with-compat --with-http_ssl_module --add-dynamic-module=/path/to/casdoor-nginx-module
make modules
cp objs/ngx_http_casdoor_module.so /etc/nginx/modules/
load_module modules/ngx_http_casdoor_module.so;

events {}

http {
    server {
        listen 443 ssl;
        server_name app.example.com;
        ssl_certificate     /etc/nginx/app.crt;
        ssl_certificate_key /etc/nginx/app.key;

        casdoor_endpoint        https://door.example.com;
        casdoor_client_id       <client-id>;
        casdoor_client_secret   <client-secret>;
        casdoor_certificate     /etc/nginx/casdoor.pem;
        casdoor_redirect_uri    https://app.example.com/casdoor/callback;
        casdoor_token_location  /_casdoor/token;

        location = /_casdoor/token {
            internal;
            proxy_pass https://door.example.com/api/login/oauth/access_token;
            proxy_ssl_server_name on;
        }

        location = /casdoor/callback {
            casdoor_callback;
        }

        location / {
            casdoor on;
            proxy_set_header X-User $casdoor_user;
            proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:3000;
        }
    }
}

Replace the placeholders with the application's values. The session isn't checked with Casdoor again until it expires, so disabling a user takes effect when the session ends; casdoor_session_timeout shortens that window. The module has no role or group checks. On NGINX Plus, see the NGINX Plus guide instead.

Option 4: the app is a CAS client​

If the app already speaks CAS, such as a Java app with the Apereo CAS client, nginx only proxies and Casdoor is the CAS server. Each Casdoor application has CAS endpoints under /cas/<organization>/<application>: /login and /logout, /validate for CAS 1.0, /serviceValidate, /proxyValidate and /proxy for 2.0, /p3/serviceValidate and /p3/proxyValidate for 3.0, and /samlValidate for SAML 1.1 validation.

The app sends the browser to /login?service=..., Casdoor redirects back with ticket=ST-..., and the app validates it:

curl "https://door.example.com/cas/my-org/my-app/p3/serviceValidate?ticket=ST-1234567890&service=https%3A%2F%2Fapp.example.com%2F"

A successful answer is a cas:serviceResponse with cas:user and attributes such as email, display name and memberOf; add format=json for JSON. Things that trip people up:

  • Every service URL must be listed in the application's Redirect URLs, and the service at validation must exactly match the one the ticket was issued for.
  • Tickets work once and expire after 5 minutes.
  • Tickets are kept in memory, so with several Casdoor replicas, validation must reach the replica that issued the ticket (sticky sessions).
  • Behind nginx, pass Host and X-Forwarded-Proto so the app builds the same service URL that the browser saw.

The setup, including the Java client's filters for each CAS version, is in Connect a CAS client.

Option 5: let Casdoor be the reverse proxy​

When nothing else sits in front of the app, Casdoor can serve it directly: its site proxy listens on gatewayHttpPort and gatewayHttpsPort (80 and 443 by default) once a site exists. Set the site's Host to the backend, pick a certificate, set Casdoor app, and point DNS at Casdoor. Login, permissions and headers behave as in option 1. See Sites.

Adding MFA​

MFA needs no change in nginx or in the app. Casdoor asks for the second factor on its own sign-in page before it issues an OAuth authorization code or a CAS service ticket, so every option above gets it. Users can use a TOTP app, SMS, email or RADIUS, with recovery codes, and administrators can require MFA for an organization with MFA items. That also answers "CAS 2FA": with Casdoor as the CAS server, the second factor is part of the CAS login.

MFA is enforced at login, not per request: a session that nginx or a forward-auth service already holds lasts until it expires, and the organization's MFA remember time lets users skip the second factor on a trusted device for a while. See the MFA guide and What is MFA.

Once signed in to Casdoor, users reach other apps that send them to Casdoor without a new password prompt; with Auto signin, Casdoor also skips the account picker. See single sign-on and Single logout.

Which one to pick​

  • No login in the app and nginx already in front: Casdoor's forward auth.
  • One login across many subdomains, or role checks per location: casdoor-forward-auth (or OAuth2 Proxy if you already run it).
  • You build nginx yourself and also protect APIs with bearer tokens: casdoor-nginx-module.
  • The app supports CAS: Casdoor's CAS endpoints, nginx as a plain proxy.
  • No proxy yet: Casdoor's site proxy.

References​

  • nginx: ngx_http_auth_request_module
  • OAuth2 Proxy: nginx integration
  • Apereo: CAS Protocol Specification, mod_auth_cas
  • Casdoor: casdoor-forward-auth, casdoor-nginx-module
  • Casdoor docs: Sites, Connect a CAS client, MFA

item.title: Spring Boot SSO with OpenID Connect: Spring Security, Resource Server and Spring Cloud Gateway with Casdoor
item.description: Add single sign-on to Spring Boot with OpenID Connect and Casdoor: oauth2Login web apps, JWT resource servers and Spring Cloud Gateway TokenRelay, with YAML.
item.content:encoded:
To add single sign-on to Spring Boot, register each app as an application in an OpenID Connect provider such as Casdoor, point Spring Security at the provider's issuer URL, and pick the Spring module that matches the app: oauth2Login() for a server-rendered web app, oauth2ResourceServer().jwt() for a REST API that receives bearer tokens, and Spring Cloud Gateway with the TokenRelay filter when one gateway signs users in for a set of microservices. Users get SSO because every app sends them to the same Casdoor, which remembers the session: the second app redirects, Casdoor already knows the user, and they come straight back without a login form. This post sets up all three shapes against one Casdoor, each with a working application.yml and a customized SecurityFilterChain.

The three shapes at a glance​

ShapeSpring dependencyWho holds the loginCasdoor endpoints usedFilter chain
Web appspring-boot-starter-oauth2-clientThe app (HTTP session)discovery, authorize, token, userinfo, JWKS, logoutSecurityFilterChain with oauth2Login()
REST APIspring-boot-starter-oauth2-resource-serverNobody, every request carries a bearer tokenJWKS (and discovery if you use issuer-uri)SecurityFilterChain with oauth2ResourceServer()
Gateway + microservicesspring-cloud-starter-gateway-server-webflux + spring-boot-starter-oauth2-clientThe gateway (WebFlux session)Same as the web app; services behind it use JWKSSecurityWebFilterChain with oauth2Login(), TokenRelay on routes

Version assumptions: Spring Boot 3.5 with Spring Security 6.5, Java 17, and Spring Cloud 2025.0 (Spring Cloud Gateway 4.3). On Spring Boot 4 the two Security starters are named spring-boot-starter-security-oauth2-client and spring-boot-starter-security-oauth2-resource-server. Gateway 4.3 and 5.0 both use the spring.cloud.gateway.server.webflux.* property prefix used below; the older spring.cloud.gateway.* prefix and the spring-cloud-starter-gateway artifact are deprecated since Spring Cloud 2025.0.

What Casdoor gives Spring​

In the Casdoor admin console, create an application (or reuse one) and copy its Client ID and Client secret. Add every callback the Spring apps will use to Redirect URLs. Spring Security's default is {baseUrl}/login/oauth2/code/{registrationId}, so with the registration ID casdoor and an app on port 8080 the URL is http://localhost:8080/login/oauth2/code/casdoor. If you use OIDC logout, also add the page users land on afterwards, for example http://localhost:8080/; Casdoor refuses a post_logout_redirect_uri that is not in the list.

Casdoor publishes a standard discovery document at /.well-known/openid-configuration, so Spring only needs the issuer. These are the endpoints it advertises, taken from the Casdoor source:

Metadata fieldCasdoor path
issuerThe backend origin, e.g. https://door.example.com (no trailing slash)
authorization_endpoint/login/oauth/authorize
token_endpoint/api/login/oauth/access_token
userinfo_endpoint/api/userinfo
jwks_uri/.well-known/jwks
end_session_endpoint/api/logout

Supported scopes are openid, email, profile, address, phone and offline_access, plus any custom scopes defined on the application. Tokens are signed with RS256 by default and carry the cert name as kid. Each application also has its own discovery document at /.well-known/<application>/openid-configuration; see Connect a standard OIDC client for the details and the full list of OAuth 2.0 endpoints.

Two things in Casdoor's tokens matter for Spring:

  • The issuer must match exactly. Spring compares the issuer in the discovery document with the issuer-uri you configure, and later with the iss claim of every token. Casdoor derives the issuer from the origin setting in app.conf, or from the Host header when origin is empty. If your Spring apps reach Casdoor through an internal hostname (say http://casdoor:8000 inside Docker) while browsers use a public one, set origin to the public URL so every token gets the same iss. See Configuration.
  • Roles come in two forms. /api/userinfo returns roles as a list of role names when the profile scope was granted. The access token in the default JWT token format contains roles as a list of role objects, each with a name field. The code below handles both. Casdoor access tokens also carry scope as a space-separated string, which Spring turns into SCOPE_... authorities by default.

If you want background on the protocol, see What is OpenID Connect and ID token vs access token.

1. Spring Boot web app with oauth2Login()​

Add spring-boot-starter-web, spring-boot-starter-security and spring-boot-starter-oauth2-client. Then configure the provider by issuer:

application.yml
server:
  port: 8080

spring:
  security:
    oauth2:
      client:
        registration:
          casdoor:
            client-id: <client-id>
            client-secret: <client-secret>
            authorization-grant-type: authorization_code
            scope: openid,profile,email
        provider:
          casdoor:
            issuer-uri: https://door.example.com
            user-name-attribute: preferred_username

At startup Spring Boot fetches https://door.example.com/.well-known/openid-configuration and fills in the authorization, token, userinfo and JWKS URIs. Spring then validates the ID token's signature, issuer, audience and nonce, calls /api/userinfo because profile and email are in the scope, and merges the claims. preferred_username is the Casdoor user name; name in userinfo is the display name, and the default sub is the user's UUID.

Without your own configuration, Spring Boot requires login for every URL. The customized SecurityFilterChain below opens the home page, maps Casdoor roles to ROLE_ authorities, and logs out of Casdoor as well as the app:

SecurityConfig.java
@Configuration
@EnableWebSecurity
public class SecurityConfig {

    @Bean
    SecurityFilterChain securityFilterChain(HttpSecurity http,
            ClientRegistrationRepository clientRegistrations) throws Exception {
        OidcClientInitiatedLogoutSuccessHandler oidcLogout =
                new OidcClientInitiatedLogoutSuccessHandler(clientRegistrations);
        oidcLogout.setPostLogoutRedirectUri("{baseUrl}/");

        http
            .authorizeHttpRequests(auth -> auth
                .requestMatchers("/", "/public/**", "/error").permitAll()
                .requestMatchers("/admin/**").hasRole("admin")
                .anyRequest().authenticated())
            .oauth2Login(login -> login
                .userInfoEndpoint(userInfo -> userInfo
                    .userAuthoritiesMapper(casdoorRoles())))
            .logout(logout -> logout
                .logoutSuccessHandler(oidcLogout));
        return http.build();
    }

    private GrantedAuthoritiesMapper casdoorRoles() {
        return authorities -> {
            Set<GrantedAuthority> mapped = new HashSet<>(authorities);
            for (GrantedAuthority authority : authorities) {
                if (authority instanceof OidcUserAuthority oidc && oidc.getUserInfo() != null) {
                    List<String> roles = oidc.getUserInfo().getClaimAsStringList("roles");
                    if (roles != null) {
                        roles.forEach(role -> mapped.add(new SimpleGrantedAuthority("ROLE_" + role)));
                    }
                }
            }
            return mapped;
        };
    }
}

hasRole("admin") now matches users who have the Casdoor role admin. OidcClientInitiatedLogoutSuccessHandler reads end_session_endpoint from the discovery document and redirects to Casdoor's /api/logout with id_token_hint and post_logout_redirect_uri, so the Casdoor session ends too. Without it, /logout only clears the Spring session and the next login is silent.

In a controller, the signed-in user is an OidcUser:

@GetMapping("/me")
Map<String, Object> me(@AuthenticationPrincipal OidcUser user) {
    return Map.of("name", user.getName(), "email", user.getEmail(),
            "authorities", user.getAuthorities().toString());
}

The older step-by-step page for this setup is Spring Security OAuth.

2. Spring Boot API as an OAuth2 resource server​

A REST API should not redirect anyone. It accepts Authorization: Bearer <access token>, checks the JWT signature against Casdoor's JWKS, and checks the claims. Add spring-boot-starter-web, spring-boot-starter-security and spring-boot-starter-oauth2-resource-server:

application.yml
server:
  port: 9000

spring:
  security:
    oauth2:
      resourceserver:
        jwt:
          issuer-uri: https://door.example.com
          jwk-set-uri: https://door.example.com/.well-known/jwks
          audiences: <client-id>

With only this file, Spring Boot builds a JwtDecoder that checks the signature, the expiry, iss and aud. Setting jwk-set-uri next to issuer-uri means the keys are fetched directly instead of through discovery, and the issuer is still validated. The audience is the client ID of the Casdoor application that issued the token: if a single-page app or the gateway from section 3 obtains the token, use that application's client ID.

There is one Casdoor-specific check worth adding. Casdoor signs ID tokens and access tokens with the same key and gives both the client ID as audience, so the default validators would also accept an ID token sent as a bearer token. Every Casdoor token has a tokenType claim (access-token, id-token or refresh-token), which makes the check simple. Defining a JwtDecoder bean replaces Boot's, so the bean re-adds the issuer and audience checks:

ApiSecurityConfig.java
@Configuration
@EnableWebSecurity
public class ApiSecurityConfig {

    @Bean
    JwtDecoder jwtDecoder(
            @Value("${spring.security.oauth2.resourceserver.jwt.issuer-uri}") String issuer,
            @Value("${spring.security.oauth2.resourceserver.jwt.jwk-set-uri}") String jwkSetUri,
            @Value("${spring.security.oauth2.resourceserver.jwt.audiences}") String clientId) {
        NimbusJwtDecoder decoder = NimbusJwtDecoder.withJwkSetUri(jwkSetUri).build();
        decoder.setJwtValidator(new DelegatingOAuth2TokenValidator<>(
                JwtValidators.createDefaultWithIssuer(issuer),
                new JwtClaimValidator<List<String>>(JwtClaimNames.AUD,
                        aud -> aud != null && aud.contains(clientId)),
                new JwtClaimValidator<String>("tokenType", "access-token"::equals)));
        return decoder;
    }

    @Bean
    SecurityFilterChain apiFilterChain(HttpSecurity http, JwtDecoder jwtDecoder) throws Exception {
        http
            .authorizeHttpRequests(auth -> auth
                .requestMatchers("/actuator/health").permitAll()
                .requestMatchers("/api/admin/**").hasRole("admin")
                .anyRequest().authenticated())
            .oauth2ResourceServer(server -> server
                .jwt(jwt -> jwt
                    .decoder(jwtDecoder)
                    .jwtAuthenticationConverter(casdoorJwtConverter())))
            .sessionManagement(session -> session
                .sessionCreationPolicy(SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESS))
            .csrf(csrf -> csrf.disable());
        return http.build();
    }

    private JwtAuthenticationConverter casdoorJwtConverter() {
        JwtGrantedAuthoritiesConverter scopes = new JwtGrantedAuthoritiesConverter();
        JwtAuthenticationConverter converter = new JwtAuthenticationConverter();
        converter.setPrincipalClaimName("name");
        converter.setJwtGrantedAuthoritiesConverter(jwt -> {
            Collection<GrantedAuthority> authorities = new ArrayList<>(scopes.convert(jwt));
            if (jwt.getClaims().get("roles") instanceof Collection<?> roles) {
                for (Object role : roles) {
                    Object name = role instanceof Map<?, ?> map ? map.get("name") : role;
                    if (name instanceof String roleName && !roleName.isEmpty()) {
                        authorities.add(new SimpleGrantedAuthority("ROLE_" + roleName));
                    }
                }
            }
            return authorities;
        });
        return converter;
    }
}

The converter keeps the SCOPE_ authorities, adds ROLE_ authorities from the roles claim whether it holds names or objects, and uses the name claim (the Casdoor user name) as the principal. If the application uses the JWT-Standard token format, use preferred_username as the principal claim instead. Disabling CSRF and sessions is right here because the API never sees a browser cookie; do not copy those two lines into the web app.

To try it without a browser, get a machine token with the client credentials grant and call the API:

TOKEN=$(curl -s -u '<client-id>:<client-secret>' \
  -d grant_type=client_credentials \
  https://door.example.com/api/login/oauth/access_token | jq -r .access_token)

curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" http://localhost:9000/api/hello

A client credentials token represents the application, not a user, so it has no roles. For more on which claims to check and why, see JWT validation and OAuth scopes.

3. Spring Cloud Gateway with TokenRelay​

With microservices, a common layout is to let the gateway handle login and keep the services as resource servers. The browser only ever talks to the gateway and holds a session cookie; the gateway stores the user's access token and the TokenRelay filter adds it as Authorization: Bearer ... to each proxied request. The services from section 2 validate it as usual.

Add spring-cloud-starter-gateway-server-webflux and spring-boot-starter-oauth2-client, with the Spring Cloud 2025.0 BOM:

application.yml
server:
  port: 8080

spring:
  application:
    name: gateway
  security:
    oauth2:
      client:
        registration:
          casdoor:
            client-id: <client-id>
            client-secret: <client-secret>
            authorization-grant-type: authorization_code
            scope: openid,profile,email
        provider:
          casdoor:
            issuer-uri: https://door.example.com
            user-name-attribute: preferred_username
  cloud:
    gateway:
      server:
        webflux:
          routes:
            - id: orders
              uri: http://localhost:9000
              predicates:
                - Path=/api/orders/**
              filters:
                - TokenRelay=
            - id: users
              uri: http://localhost:9001
              predicates:
                - Path=/api/users/**
              filters:
                - TokenRelay=

TokenRelay= with no argument relays the token of the signed-in user. The TokenRelay filter factory is only created when spring.security.oauth2.client.* is configured, and the default authorized-client store is in memory, so a gateway with several replicas needs a shared store or sticky sessions. The services behind it set audiences to the gateway's client ID.

Spring Cloud Gateway runs on WebFlux, so its security configuration is a SecurityWebFilterChain built from ServerHttpSecurity, not the servlet SecurityFilterChain:

GatewaySecurityConfig.java
@Configuration
@EnableWebFluxSecurity
public class GatewaySecurityConfig {

    @Bean
    SecurityWebFilterChain gatewayFilterChain(ServerHttpSecurity http,
            ReactiveClientRegistrationRepository clientRegistrations) {
        OidcClientInitiatedServerLogoutSuccessHandler oidcLogout =
                new OidcClientInitiatedServerLogoutSuccessHandler(clientRegistrations);
        oidcLogout.setPostLogoutRedirectUri("{baseUrl}/");

        http
            .authorizeExchange(exchanges -> exchanges
                .pathMatchers("/", "/actuator/health").permitAll()
                .anyExchange().authenticated())
            .oauth2Login(Customizer.withDefaults())
            .logout(logout -> logout.logoutSuccessHandler(oidcLogout));
        return http.build();
    }
}

Keep authorization decisions in the services, where the roles are in the token; the gateway only makes sure there is a signed-in user. CSRF protection stays on in the gateway because it is cookie-based.

The existing Spring Cloud Gateway and Spring Cloud pages show a different design, where a custom GlobalFilter checks a Casdoor user stored in the gateway session.

Alternative: the Casdoor Spring Boot starter​

If you would rather not write the YAML, casdoor-spring-boot-starter 2.x (Spring Boot 3 and 4, Java 17+) takes casdoor.endpoint, casdoor.client-id, casdoor.client-secret, casdoor.organization-name and casdoor.application-name, and sets the spring.security.oauth2.* properties above for whichever Security starter is on the classpath. It registers the client as casdoor, maps Casdoor roles to ROLE_ authorities for both OAuth2 login and the servlet resource server, and exposes the Casdoor Java SDK services as beans. Its properties have the lowest precedence, so you can still override any of them. See Spring Boot for the setup.

Common errors​

  • "The Issuer ... provided in the configuration metadata did not match the requested issuer": the issuer-uri differs from what Casdoor reports. Remove any trailing slash, and set origin in Casdoor if the hostnames differ.
  • redirect_uri rejected by Casdoor: the callback is not in the application's Redirect URLs. Check the scheme and port, especially behind a reverse proxy.
  • "Missing attribute 'preferred_username'": the profile scope was not requested, or the application's token fields leave out Name.
  • 401 with an invalid_token error on the API: the token came from another application (wrong aud), it is expired, or it is an ID token.

References​

  • Casdoor discovery document and endpoints: object/wellknown_oidc_discovery.go
  • Casdoor token claims: object/token_jwt.go
  • Spring Boot 3.5 reference: Spring Security, OAuth2 client and resource server
  • Spring Security: OIDC client-initiated logout
  • Spring Security: OAuth 2.0 resource server JWT
  • Spring Cloud Gateway: TokenRelay GatewayFilter factory
  • Spring Cloud Gateway: starter spring-cloud-starter-gateway-server-webflux
  • Spring Cloud 2025.0 release notes
  • casdoor-spring-boot-starter

item.title: Casdoor v4 : une nouvelle console, un Marketplace et OAuth pour les serveurs MCP
item.description: Casdoor v4.0 est sorti le 1er septembre. Deux mois et 25 versions plus tard, nous en sommes à la v4.25 ; c'est donc le bon moment pour revenir sur ce qui a changé. En résumé : la console d'administration a été reconstruite, l'auto-hébergement est devenu beaucoup moins fastidieux, il existe désormais un Marketplace pour les intégrations et les thèmes de connexion, et Casdoor peut agir comme serveur d'autorisation pour les serveurs MCP et les agents IA.
item.content:encoded:
Casdoor v4.0 est sorti le 1er septembre. Deux mois et 25 versions plus tard, nous en sommes à la v4.25 ; c'est donc le bon moment pour revenir sur ce qui a changé. En résumé : la console d'administration a été reconstruite, l'auto-hébergement est devenu beaucoup moins fastidieux, il existe désormais un Marketplace pour les intégrations et les thèmes de connexion, et Casdoor peut agir comme serveur d'autorisation pour les serveurs MCP et les agents IA.

Si vous ne l'avez jamais utilisé : Casdoor est une plateforme open-source de gestion des identités et des accès (IAM) écrite en Go. C'est un fournisseur d'identité complet, pas une bibliothèque ni un proxy de connexion. Les utilisateurs résident dans Casdoor, Casdoor émet les jetons, et vos applications communiquent avec lui via OAuth 2.0, OpenID Connect, SAML 2.0, CAS, LDAP ou SCIM. L'autorisation est gérée par Apache Casbin, de sorte que les modèles ACL, RBAC et ABAC fonctionnent tous. Il est sous licence Apache-2.0 et figure dans le CNCF Landscape.

Une console et des pages de connexion reconstruites​

La v4.0 a remplacé la console d'administration Ant Design par une nouvelle construite avec shadcn/ui, Tailwind et Vite (actuellement sur React 19). Elle dispose d'une palette de commandes, de la sélection multiple de lignes, de la validation de formulaire en ligne, de formulaires et tableaux à deux colonnes où vous pouvez masquer des colonnes. Le changement de langue ne recharge plus la page.

Les pages de connexion, d'inscription et de réinitialisation du mot de passe ont également été redessinées. Le mode sombre fonctionne correctement, et les pages sont utilisables sur un téléphone.

Si vous effectuez une mise à niveau depuis la v3, consultez d'abord le guide de mise à niveau lié depuis le README. La principale chose à vérifier est le chemin de la compilation frontend si vous servez des fichiers statiques via un CDN ou un reverse proxy.

Un auto-hébergement simplifié​

Une grande partie du travail de la v4 provient des tickets et des fils de forum de personnes hébergeant elles-mêmes Casdoor :

  • Pas de mot de passe par défaut. Lors de la première visite, Casdoor vous demande de définir le mot de passe admin, ou vous pouvez le définir via initAdminPassword.
  • Déploiement sur un sous-chemin. Définissez basePath pour servir Casdoor à https://example.com/auth/ au lieu de son propre hôte.
  • Forward auth. Casdoor dispose d'un point de terminaison forward auth pour Traefik, Caddy et Nginx, ce qui vous permet de placer derrière lui des applications n'ayant pas leur propre système de connexion, avec des chemins publics et des règles par site.
  • Tags Docker. Les images sont désormais également taguées X, X.Y et X.Y.Z, afin que vous puissiez suivre une version majeure ou mineure.
  • Helm. Le chart a été déplacé dans le dépôt principal, est publié sur GHCR et Artifact Hub à chaque release, et peut conserver les organisations, les applications et les utilisateurs comme configuration. Voir Exécution de Casdoor sur Kubernetes.
  • Service Windows. Le binaire peut s'exécuter en tant que service Windows.
  • Mises à jour. La page d'informations système affiche la dernière release et peut mettre à jour un binaire officiel en un clic.
  • Opérations. Vérifications de santé des conteneurs, compteurs Prometheus pour les succès et échecs de connexion, logs d'audit transmis vers Syslog, et prise en charge de Redis Cluster.

Marketplace​

Le nouveau Marketplace permet à un administrateur d'installer des intégrations directement depuis Casdoor : modèles d'applications, fournisseurs d'identité et thèmes de connexion. L'installation préremplit la configuration pour vous, et la désinstallation restaure la configuration précédente.

Il y a actuellement plus de 20 thèmes de connexion. Vous pouvez prévisualiser un thème sur votre propre page de connexion avant de l'installer. Les administrateurs d'organisation peuvent également personnaliser les pages de connexion avec leurs propres polices, images et HTML, dans le cadre d'une liste blanche qui bloque les formulaires et les scripts. La démo en lecture seule sur door.casdoor.com fait défiler les thèmes si vous souhaitez les voir.

OAuth pour les serveurs MCP et les agents IA​

La spécification MCP demande aux serveurs MCP distants d'utiliser OAuth, et les clients MCP ne connaissent généralement pas à l'avance quel serveur d'autorisation ils rencontreront. Casdoor couvre désormais les éléments nécessaires :

  • Flux de code d'autorisation OAuth 2.1 avec PKCE, et une page de consentement où les utilisateurs peuvent n'accorder qu'une partie des scopes demandés
  • Enregistrement dynamique des clients (RFC 7591) et gestion des clients (RFC 7592)
  • Client ID Metadata Documents : un client MCP peut utiliser une URL comme client_id sans s'enregistrer au préalable
  • Authentification du client private_key_jwt pour les clients enregistrés dynamiquement
  • Indicateurs de ressource (RFC 8707) et métadonnées des ressources protégées (RFC 9728)
  • Échange de jeton (RFC 8693), y compris les ID-JAGs pour l'autorisation gérée par l'entreprise, afin que l'IdP d'une organisation puisse décider quels agents peuvent accéder à quels serveurs MCP

Pointez les métadonnées de la ressource protégée de votre serveur MCP vers Casdoor, et la connexion, le consentement, l'émission et la validation des jetons sont gérés pour vous. Casdoor exécute également son propre serveur MCP, afin qu'un assistant tel que Claude Code ou Cursor puisse gérer les utilisateurs, les applications et les autorisations via celui-ci.

Autres travaux sur les protocoles​

  • SAML Single Logout et SSO initié par l'IdP
  • OIDC prompt=none, meilleure conformité pour le flux hybride, prompt et max_age, et le paramètre iss de la RFC 9207
  • Révocation de jeton (RFC 7009), DPoP et le flux d'autorisation d'appareil
  • Connexion par lien magique, vérification de l'historique des mots de passe, et passkeys partagés entre sous-domaines frères
  • Connexion exclusive avec un nombre maximum de sessions par utilisateur

Essayer​

Le moyen le plus rapide d'explorer :

docker run -p 8000:8000 casbin/casdoor-all-in-one

Ouvrez ensuite http://localhost:8000. L'image inclut SQLite et des données d'exemple, utilisez-la donc pour essayer, pas pour la production. Le guide d'installation couvre les déploiements réels.

Il existe deux démos en ligne : demo.casdoor.com est modifiable et se réinitialise toutes les cinq minutes, et door.casdoor.com est en lecture seule.

Si vous préférez ne pas l'héberger vous-même, Casdoor Cloud vous offre une instance dédiée et managée à prix forfaitaire sans frais par utilisateur. Les nouveaux comptes reçoivent 10 $ de crédit pour l'essayer.

Liens​

  • GitHub : https://github.com/casdoor/casdoor
  • Notes de version : https://github.com/casdoor/casdoor/releases
  • Docs : https://casdoor.ai/docs/overview
  • Discord : https://discord.gg/5rPsrAzK7S

Les rapports de bugs et les demandes de fonctionnalités sont bienvenus sur GitHub. Si Casdoor vous est utile, une étoile aide d'autres personnes à le trouver.

item.title: Exécution de Casdoor sur Kubernetes : Helm Chart officiel et Configuration as Code
item.description: Casdoor dispose d'un Helm chart officiel. Il se trouve dans le dépôt principal sous manifests/casdoor, est publié avec chaque version de Casdoor sur GHCR, et est référencé sur Artifact Hub. À partir de Casdoor v4.18.0, le chart peut également contenir vos organisations, applications, utilisateurs et fournisseurs comme configuration déclarative : modifiez-les dans le fichier values, exécutez helm upgrade, et les pods en cours appliquent la modification sans redémarrage.
item.content:encoded:
Casdoor dispose d'un Helm chart officiel. Il se trouve dans le dépôt principal sous manifests/casdoor, est publié avec chaque version de Casdoor sur GHCR, et est référencé sur Artifact Hub. À partir de Casdoor v4.18.0, le chart peut également contenir vos organisations, applications, utilisateurs et fournisseurs comme configuration déclarative : modifiez-les dans le fichier values, exécutez helm upgrade, et les pods en cours appliquent la modification sans redémarrage.

Cet article détaille un déploiement Kubernetes depuis le premier helm install jusqu'à une configuration que vous pouvez conserver dans Git.

Installation​

Vous avez besoin de Helm v3.8+ et d'un cluster :

helm install casdoor oci://ghcr.io/casdoor/helm-charts/casdoor

La version du chart correspond à la version de Casdoor, donc --version 4.18.0 installe Casdoor 4.18.0. Sans Ingress ou Gateway, le service n'est accessible qu'à l'intérieur du cluster. Pour tester, transférez un port :

kubectl port-forward svc/casdoor 8000:8000

Puis ouvrez http://localhost:8000. Lors de la première visite, Casdoor vous demande de définir le mot de passe de built-in/admin ; connectez-vous ensuite avec celui-ci. Voir Se connecter à la console d'administration.

Une configuration de production​

Les paramètres par défaut sont destinés à un essai rapide : Casdoor stocke ses données dans SQLite à l'intérieur du conteneur, elles sont donc perdues lorsque le pod est remplacé. Pour un déploiement réel, placez les paramètres ci-dessous dans un fichier values.yaml et installez avec helm install casdoor oci://ghcr.io/casdoor/helm-charts/casdoor -f values.yaml.

Base de données externe​

database:
  driver: postgres # or mysql, cockroachdb
  host: postgres.db.svc.cluster.local
  user: casdoor
  password: change-me
  databaseName: casdoor
  sslMode: require

Pour éviter de placer le mot de passe de la base de données dans le fichier values, mettez tout le app.conf dans un Secret et définissez configFromSecret sur son nom.

Exposer Casdoor​

Le chart supporte à la fois un Ingress classique et l'API Gateway. Avec un contrôleur Ingress et cert-manager :

ingress:
  enabled: true
  className: nginx
  annotations:
    cert-manager.io/cluster-issuer: letsencrypt-prod
  hosts:
    - host: door.example.com
      paths:
        - path: /
          pathType: Prefix
  tls:
    - secretName: casdoor-tls
      hosts:
        - door.example.com

Avec l'API Gateway (Istio, Envoy Gateway, Cilium, Kong, NGINX Gateway Fabric et autres), attachez une HTTPRoute à une Gateway existante :

gatewayApi:
  enabled: true
  parentRefs:
    - name: my-gateway
      namespace: gateway-system
  hostnames:
    - door.example.com

Le chart peut également créer la Gateway lui-même et ajouter une redirection HTTP vers HTTPS, voir le guide Helm.

Plusieurs répliques​

Par défaut, Casdoor conserve les sessions de connexion sur le disque local. Avant d'exécuter plusieurs répliques, pointez toutes les instances vers le même Redis, afin qu'un utilisateur reste connecté quel que soit le pod servant la requête. Chaque paramètre app.conf peut être passé comme variable d'environnement, donc le point d'accès peut provenir d'un Secret :

replicaCount: 3

envFromSecret:
  - name: redisEndpoint
    secretName: casdoor-redis
    key: endpoint # host:port, or host:port,db,password

Le même Redis est utilisé pour l'état du flux de périphérique OAuth. Une fois Redis en place, autoscaling.enabled: true ajoute un HorizontalPodAutoscaler.

Configuration as code​

Cliquer pour assembler les organisations et les applications dans l'interface web convient pour un premier test, mais la plupart des équipes souhaitent que la configuration de leur fournisseur d'identité soit revue et versionnée comme le reste de leur infrastructure. Les valeurs initData permettent cela :

initData:
  enabled: true
  data:
    organizations:
      - owner: admin
        name: acme
        displayName: Acme
        passwordType: bcrypt
    applications:
      - owner: admin
        name: app-acme-portal
        organization: acme
        displayName: Acme Portal
        redirectUris:
          - https://portal.acme.example.com/callback
    users:
      - owner: acme
        name: alice
        displayName: Alice
        password: change-me
        signupApplication: app-acme-portal
    roles:
      - owner: acme
        name: admins
        displayName: Admins
        users: [acme/alice]
        isEnabled: true

Le chart stocke les données dans un Secret et les monte dans les pods. Casdoor les applique au démarrage, puis les vérifie toutes les 30 secondes (initData.watchInterval). Lorsque vous modifiez les données et exécutez helm upgrade, kubelet met à jour le Secret monté et les pods en cours l'appliquent sans redémarrage.

Quelques règles rendent cette utilisation sûre aux côtés de l'interface web :

  • Seuls les champs que vous écrivez sont gérés. Un objet existant reçoit les champs définis dans le fichier ; ses autres champs conservent les valeurs éditées dans l'interface. Vous pouvez gérer uniquement les URI de redirection d'une application, et laisser le reste à la console d'administration.
  • Les mots de passe sont des mots de passe initiaux. Le password d'un utilisateur n'est utilisé que lors de la création de l'utilisateur, ce qui permet aux utilisateurs de le modifier par la suite.
  • Rien n'est supprimé. La suppression d'un objet du fichier ne le supprime pas de Casdoor.
  • Les erreurs n'arrêtent pas Casdoor. Si l'application d'un objet échoue, l'erreur est journalisée et Casdoor continue de fonctionner ; les données sont réessayées à chaque vérification jusqu'à leur application réussie.

Le format du fichier est celui que Casdoor a toujours utilisé pour l'initialisation des données : organisations, applications, utilisateurs, fournisseurs, certificats, rôles, permissions, groupes, serveurs LDAP, webhooks, plans, tarifs et plus encore, avec les mêmes noms de champs que l'API REST. Une façon rapide de démarrer consiste à exporter une instance existante avec casdoor -export et à conserver les objets que vous souhaitez gérer.

Pour garder les données hors du fichier values, par exemple lorsqu'elles sont gérées par Sealed Secrets ou External Secrets, créez vous-même le Secret :

initData:
  enabled: true
  existingSecret: casdoor-init-data
  existingSecretKey: init_data.yaml

La même fonctionnalité fonctionne sans Kubernetes. Montez un fichier JSON ou YAML et définissez :

initDataFile = /init-data/init_data.yaml
initDataMerge = true
initDataWatchInterval = 30

Ou utilisez Terraform​

Si vous préférez terraform plan, l'importation d'objets existants et la détection de dérives, le provider Terraform officiel gère les mêmes objets via l'API Casdoor :

resource "casdoor_application" "portal" {
  name          = "app-acme-portal"
  organization  = "acme"
  redirect_uris = ["https://portal.acme.example.com/callback"]
}

Utilisez les valeurs Helm lorsque la configuration doit être livrée avec le déploiement, et Terraform lorsque Casdoor fait partie de nombreux systèmes que vous gérez déjà avec lui. Consultez le guide Terraform.

Migration depuis l'ancien chart​

Jusqu'à la v4.15.0, le chart était publié sous oci://registry-1.docker.io/casbin/casdoor-helm-charts, et le dépôt séparé casdoor/casdoor-helm est désormais archivé. Le chart Docker Hub reçoit toujours chaque nouvelle version, mais les nouvelles installations doivent utiliser celui hébergé sur GHCR. Migrer une release existante est une mise à niveau classique, et les noms des ressources restent inchangés :

helm upgrade casdoor oci://ghcr.io/casdoor/helm-charts/casdoor --version <version>

Liens​

  • Chart Helm : Artifact Hub · source
  • Guides : Essayer avec Helm · Initialisation des données et configuration as code · Terraform
  • Vous ne souhaitez pas le gérer vous-même ? Casdoor Cloud vous offre une instance Casdoor dédiée que nous hébergeons et maintenons à jour pour vous.

Le 22 février 2026, Casdoor a rejoint le CNCF Cloud Native Landscape, dans la catégorie Security & Compliance sous Provisioning. Le Landscape regroupe des projets et produits cloud-natifs largement utilisés ; son inclusion aide les utilisateurs et les entreprises à découvrir et évaluer des solutions pour construire des systèmes cloud-natifs.

https://landscape.cncf.io/?item=provisioning--security-compliance--casdoor

Casdoor on the CNCF Cloud Native Landscape (Security & Compliance)

À propos de Casdoor​

Casdoor est une plateforme open-source, orientée interface utilisateur, de gestion des identités et des accès (IAM) / d'authentification unique (SSO) avec une interface web. Elle prend en charge OAuth 2.0, OIDC, SAML et CAS, ainsi que de nombreuses connexions sociales (Google, GitHub, WeChat, etc.), et vous aide à mettre en place la gestion des utilisateurs et le SSO en quelques étapes. Casdoor est développé par Casbin en Golang et React. Il utilise une architecture séparant le front-end du back-end, supporte la haute concurrence et est activement maintenu par la communauté. Le projet a reçu plus de 13k étoiles GitHub.

À propos de CNCF et du Cloud Native Landscape​

La Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF) est un projet de la Linux Foundation qui promeut les technologies cloud-natives. Sa vision est de rendre le cloud natif omniprésent. La CNCF maintient le Cloud Native Landscape (https://landscape.cncf.io), qui classe et suit les projets et produits dans l'écosystème cloud-native et sert de carte de référence pour les développeurs et les entreprises.

Perspectives d'avenir​

Rejoindre le CNCF Landscape reflète les progrès de la maturité de Casdoor et de sa communauté. Nous continuerons à améliorer Casdoor et son intégration avec les workflows cloud-natifs, et nous accueillons avec plaisir davantage d'utilisateurs et de contributeurs pour rejoindre la communauté.
